Comparing all AI investment as one speculative bubble is rather like analysing the telecom boom without distinguishing between Cisco, Vodafone, BT, WorldCom and Global Crossing. They were all participants in the same revolution, but they had very different business models, funding structures, risks and motivations.


Much of the current discussion around AI suffers from the same weakness that characterised commentary during the telecom boom: treating a complex ecosystem as though it were a single trade. During the telecom era, network operators, equipment suppliers, infrastructure builders and service providers were often discussed as one industry, despite having vastly different business models, capital requirements and risks. The result was analysis that frequently conflated technological success with investment success.

The AI landscape is similarly diverse. OpenAI and Anthropic are venture-backed challengers attempting to become the next dominant platforms. Google and Microsoft are investing not simply because competitors are spending, but because AI has the potential to reshape the profit pools that underpin their existing businesses. Amazon occupies a different position again, supplying much of the infrastructure on which the wider AI ecosystem depends. Nvidia, meanwhile, resembles the equipment providers of the telecom era, benefiting from the build-out regardless of which applications ultimately prevail.

The telecom boom demonstrated that a technology can be genuinely transformative while at the same time proving financially disastrous for many participants. The world did not need less fibre; it needed fewer companies building competing networks financed by excessive debt. The mistake for many was not overestimating the importance of communications infrastructure, but underestimating the intensity of competition and the difficulty of capturing economic returns.

The same distinction applies to AI. Aggregate capital expenditure figures tell us very little on their own. What matters is not simply who is spending, but why they are spending, how they are financing that spending, whether they are defending an existing franchise or creating a new one, and whether they possess durable advantages that allow them to capture the value being created.

The question, therefore, is not whether AI is a bubble or a revolution. The telecom boom was both. The more important question is which participants are building lasting economic value, which are merely funding industry-wide infrastructure, and who ultimately captures the returns from one of the largest technology build-outs in modern history.

11:43 for anyone interested in what a token actually is:

LLMs only deal with numbers. So they have to convert words to numbers. They have to have a completely fixed set of possible numbers that can go in or out. This is because the actual output of the model is a list of all the possible numbers (referring to words or tokens) and a probability (how likely each is to be the correct next word).

We could use full words, but there are a lot of words, and the list would be ridiculously long, which makes it bad.

We could split them into letters, but then the model has to be trained how to predict letters in the correct order to make words, which also makes it bad.

So we compromise and split words up into their common parts, called tokenisation. For example, "hello" probably just becomes "hello", whereas "bookshelf" becomes "book" and "shelf".

text:
AI is useful, but its not as world changing as promised at this point. I dont think discounting the use cases is especially useful to the economic argument. So here's my honest experience:

I'm a mechanical engineer. I design stuff, have it made, run experiments, analyze the data. The only task there I've really used it for is data analysis (claude). It coded up some neat python scripts for me. It still took a week, and a skilled coder could probably do it faster, but it allowed me to do something that wasn't in my normal skill set. Neat.

What it really helps with is the soft stuff. I have to write a report, generate a monthly schedule, make a process control document. It is terribly dumb at filling in the material itself, and the phrasing is so obviously AI, but I get it to generate a good template and then I can ask for more detail about what should go where. Probably makes me 30-50% more efficient with those tasks, about 5-10% overall. 

That's my 2 cents based on my experience. In certain fields of science its probably more useful, in a job with a lot of document generation its probably more useful. But in anything public facing or that will undergo technical scrutiny you need probably 2 layers of human vetting between it and release. Its just not that good. 

Oh, the advanced search (google) I've found really useful for troubleshooting. Computer error codes, car issues. Much better than scrolling forums. So definite value there.

As for stagnation of technology, absolutely. What's changed in the last 10-15 years? Had a smart phone then, have one now that does the same thing. We have smart light bulbs now, but do they make the room any brighter? Things are getting marginally better/faster/efficient, but TV resolutions are saturated. Video game graphics are almost photorealistic. Tech is in this dismissing returns curve, where leaps and improvements are really marginal.
